speechtext:
I am glad that the old-established tradition of parliament, to debate the address in reply to the speech from the throne, has not been abandoned this year. It has been the custom from time immemorial, at the opening of parliament, to allow the house to express itself on the conditions prevailing in the country, and I have been long enough in public life to have the highest respect for these old conditions and customs which have been sanctioned by the experience of ages.
I regret that at this time the ministry has not seen fit to take part in this debate. I know that many lion, gentlemen opposite would have many things to say were they given an opportunity to address the house at the present time. But we have been told by the Prime Minister that the reason for our meeting now is merely for the purpose of legislating upon the enactments brought about by the Imperial economic conference, and nothing more. Of course, that may be his view of the situation, but unfortunately we represent the people at large, and the people at large do not wish us to deal with one thing only to the neglect of everything else. We are here as the representatives of all classes and sections of the country. Many, no doubt, are interested in the outcome of this conference and the negotiations in connection therewith, but at the present time there are conditions in this country which it is the duty of the elected representatives of the people to make known and to bring to the attention of their colleagues and of the government of the day.
No doubt great importance is being attached to the holding of the Imperial conference here, which is, in a way, another indication of what has taken place in the last few years in the rapid strides that have been made in constitutional government in this country and in the empire at large. The speech from the throne, which we are called upon to discuss, contains certain statements which enable me to refer to other matters besides the conference. It being understood that the resolutions adopted at that conference and the proposals made are to be taken up next week, I do not think it is either right or proper that I should refer to them now, but I cannot refrain from reference to the first paragraph of the address, which concludes with these words:
My government are of opinion that these agreements provide the means by which will be developed an enduring and mutually beneficial scheme of closer empire economic association, and that their early approval is advisable In the national interest.

The Address-Mr. Marcil

There is no doubt that that should be brought about as speedily as possible consistent with our duty towards the people and towards those who are chiefly interested. Taking up an evening paper, a strong supporter of the government, I find the following headline: "General approval given new trade agreements." The first article under this headline contains the following:
J. E. Walsh, general manager of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, is in Ottawa today but he declined to make any general comment, expressing the belief that the tariff changes were so varied that it would be better for spokesmen in the different Canadian industries affected to discuss them.
When a man of this character, the manager of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, a man who has given up the whole of his time year after year to the study of tariffs, is unable to give a pronouncement at the present time, it is almost impossible for a member of this house to come to a conclusion as to the value of the proposals now before us. Statements to the same effect appear in other papers. I have one before me from a Montreal paper which gives the viewpoint of industry. It reads:
Practically all executives of leading companies which have been affected by the changes in the Canadian tariff announced at Ottawa today declined to comment, pleading the need of further study before a just appraisal could be made.	.
The generous extension of the British preferential tariff was generally hailed as a constructive step in building up reciprocal empire trade. It was agreed that there would be some effect on leading Canadian industries such as steel, textiles, distilleries, glass and tobacco, but there was no indication given that sound Canadian industries would suffer any serious adverse effect by the change.
That is the opinion of one group in Montreal, but in an adjoining column of the same paper there appears a statement of the manager of a Cornwall cotton mill, to the effect that the only way in which Canadian cotton mills will be able to compete favourably with British mills will 'be by a reduction in the wages of the working man. The statement has been made by an executive of a large woollen mill in Ontario to the effect that production may have to be contracted because in certain lines competition with the people on the other side of the water will be almost impossible.
This is an old story. Tariffs do not suit everybody; they never did and they never will. If they could suit a majority of the people it would be something, but tariffs have been discussed for many years in Canada and in the country to the south without arriving at

a satisfactory conclusion. Today the tariff is the outstanding question before the people of the United States.
Last night I listened at the radio for an hour and three-quarters to a speech delivered by the President of the United States at Des Moines, Iowa, in defence of the American tariff. It seemed almost incredible to me that a man of that calibre, the leader of
120.000.	000 people, should take up an hour and three-quarters in the defence of a policy which has almost brought the United States to the brink of ruin. There are to-day nearly
14.000.	000 unemployed in the United States which means that almost 60,000,000, or one-half the population, is affected. This condition has been brought about because of the high tariff policy of that country.
From 1897 to 1911, under the regime of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, this country experienced the most prosperous period in its history and it seems almost incredible that we have not benefited by the experience of the United States. That country closed its doors to the commerce of the world and now it is feeling the effect. We imitated its actions during the short session of 1930 and as I listened yesterday to the great effort made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) I could not help but realize that he was trying to undo what he had done in September, 1930. At that time we closed our markets to the other countries of the world; we sold practically nothing and imported very little. When you do not sell, you do not buy. Our total trade has been declining at the rate of almost $2,000,000 per day since the new tariff changes were put into effect and I wonder how the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) will take care of this loss of revenue when he presents his budget next year.
It is expected that these new' agreements will permit from 875,000,000 to 8100,000,000 worth of goods to come in from England free of duty and this will necessitate our finding revenue somewhere else. It is no use trying to disguise the fact that we are trying to displace trade with the United States by trade with England. England is our motherland, we are all proud of being British subjects- I come from a part of the country where the people pride themselves upon the fact that they will remain forever loyal to the British crown: they are determined to do this for many reasons which I shall not enumerate at the present time-but we must realize that our natural market is the United States. Whatever trade w'e may have with England

The Address-Mr. Marcil
and other parts of the empire it will never offset the trade which we should have with the United States.
At one time the Liberal party under its great leader attempted to bring about a better understanding with the country to the south in order that we might have at hand a market for our natural products. The Canadian people were misled by such questions as the imperial navy, contributions to the empire and so on, and they voted against reciprocity. It has been recognized in all parts of the country that that was a fatal mistake because we lost our natural market. The American people have gone to the other extreme; they have gone so far that there is bound to be a change in government on November 8. If I read aright the feelings of the people, there is bound to be a great change in the next elections in the United States. The people cannot stand the exclusion which that country has placed upon the goods of other countries, to such an extent that 67 other countries have followed in its footsteps.
I am old enough in politics to hope that the results of this conference will prove to be a success. The country is really in a bad state at the present time. During my fifty-five years of public life I have had many experiences with depressions but even the great depression of 1878 was not a drop in the bucket compared with the one today. At that time I was living in the city of Montreal, the largest city in the dominion with a population of 225,000; during those days we had soup kitchens and so on, but the general situation brought about the downfall of Alexander Mackenzie, the man who did not want to tax the people because there was no necessity for taxation. But the condition in those days was nothing compared with what it is today. At the present time I am informed that in the city of Montreal there are
125,000	people receiving relief. What will the figure be next year? What position will they be in in that large city? At the present time ten per cent of the population are receiving relief either from the Dominion or from the municipality or from the province of Quebec. The same thing applies throughout the Dominion, the figure having been placed at
700,000.	The Prime Minister is very sanguine of the success of these negotiations he has had with the mother country and the other dominions of the empire. But he says: These are potentialities; we shall control the bacon market in England provided that we are equipped for that and we are able to displace Holland, Denmark and the other countries that now control that market. That may
take time. In some cases he talked about three years and in others about five years. We have to displace Argentina and other countries, for instance the Irish Free State, and so on, that are near to the mother country. Are we able to do that? Are we going to imagine we shall be able to displace those countries no matter what preferences are given to us? I doubt this very much, but I hope for the best; I hope some good will come out of these negotiations. Until, however, we have sifted them to the bottom, no man seems competent to express an opinion. We have heard the opinions of technical men but at present I do not wish to express an opinion.
In the meantime I feel it my duty to bring to the attention of the house certain conditions which prevail in my constituency, thereby giving an idea of what prevails throughout the rest of the country. In the last campaign in 1930, in the month of July, my opponent of course re-echoed the promises made by his leader. He was amazed, dumbfounded and almost scandalized by the terrible New Zealand butter treaty. The good farmers of Bonaventure county on the day they voted, large numbers of them for the Conservative party, were selling their butter at 36 cents per pound. Last summer butter in that county netted the farmer 9t cents per pound; he was paid 4 cents a gallon for his milk, and money is so scarce that they are unable to pay their taxes, unable in many cases to pay the pews they have in the church and unable to pay their school teachers. The question is whether the schools can be kept open; never before in the thirty years that I have represented that county have I seen such a state of affairs as exists there at the present time. Fishermen told me that at the end of June they crossed the Baie des Chaleurs in their sailing boats and purchased grade No. 1 potatoes for 25 and 20 cents a barrel, bringing them back for local consumption. This was last year's crop, which was being replaced by the new crop coming in. Some got them even as low as 15 cents a barrel. We have had no shanties in eastern Quebec for the last two years. Thousands and thousands of our young men who every year go into the lumber woods were idle last winter and the winter before, and they are going to be idle again this winter. Every saw mill from Rimouski down the Matapedia valley along the coast of Bonaventure and Gaspe has been closed, with one exception. The hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Lacroix) has a saw mill where he is sawing a quantity of logs so that they will not be completely lost, but he says
1S2
The Address-Mr. Marcil

that he can find no market for his product. Therefore in the lumber industry there has been complete stagnation. In the town of Campbellton, which is the leading town of northern New Brunswick, all the mills with one exception are closed down; between three and four thousand men are idle and the people do not know where to turn and how to get food and clothing during the coming winter. We all received some days ago two or three slices of bread that were sent to us by mail-bread for the chomeurs, for the unemployed. Those are the rations that are being given to good Canadians who are willing to work. If this government could implement only half the promises it made and find a market for our farmers and work for our mechanics, all our troubles would be settled. In the city of Ottawa market produce has been practically given away during the summer. Large baskets of beautiful tomatoes have been sold at ten cents a basket. I shall say no more about the present situation, because when these economic proposals are under consideration I shall be in a position to discuss them with better knowledge than I have at the present moment.
In the second paragraph of the speech from the throne I find the statement that during the present session legislation will be introduced to give effect to certain recommendations of the transportation commission. With all the respect that I have for the members of this commission, some of whom are railway men, others judges and others bankers, their findings are merely their own opinions, and I hate to imagine that they are more competent to express an opinion than Mr. Beatty or Sir Henry Thornton. We shall, however, judge what the government decides to accept of those recommendations when the bill is brought in. There has no doubt been superabundance of railway construction in this country; too many railways have been built, but I still hear speeches that were uttered in this chamber twenty or twenty-five years ago by members from western Canada who, when in 1904 we decided upon the construction of the transcontinental, claimed that it was not one or two transcontinental railways that would be needed in the west, but that half a dozen railways would be required. Men of the standing of Clifford Sifton and others of both parties coming from the west were confident that the words of Sir Charles Tupper had come true and that western Canada had in fact become the granary of the world. They were insistent in the matter, and some years later when I had the honour of occupy-(Mr. Marcil.]
ing the chair which you, sir, now have the honour to occupy, I listened to western members of both political parties insisting on the immediate construction of the Hudson Bay railway and I do not know how many other branch lines in addition. Of course those people were confident of the future of Canada; they were confident that the prosperity which existed under the Laurier regime, when a thousand immigrants came into Canada every day, when every train to the west was filled with immigrants and every steamer from overseas was bringing new citizens to this country, would continue. But unfortunately it did not.
In 1911 there was a change and the change was not for the better. Then the unfortunate period of the war came and that made matters still worse. But what position was the Liberal party in when in 1921 it took office? We all remember the railway situation that prevailed. The Canadian National Railway is the creation of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, who took part in many an ardent debate with the present leader of the government. When the proposals were made in the house that the Canadian Northern be taken over, the present leader of the government was not quite in agreement with the then Prime Minister. Be that as it may, the Conservative party claimed, and rightly so to a certain extent, that the Canadian National was their creation, and they were proud of their offspring. When the Liberal party came into power we were divided on the question. Some were in favour of public ownership; others were in favour of private ownership. Private ownership has been a success; the Canadian Pacific Railway is one of the outstanding companies of the world; it will sell you a ticket which will take you to the other end of the world. It controls business not only on land but on the five seas. Public ownership also has something to its credit, in the province of Ontario it has been a success, in the province of Quebec we have private ownership, that is the desire of the people. In the United States opinions are divided, in some parts they favour public ownership, in other parts private ownership.
In 1921 the Liberal party decided to give public ownership a fair trial, and we scanned the world for an outstanding man who could take charge of the defunct, bankrupt, broken-down railway system that we had at that time. Such a man was found in the person of Sir Henry Thornton. His coming into Canada was acclaimed. Things were prosperous, we were paying off our debts, we had

The Address-Mr. Marcil
surpluses, we were bringing down taxation, that was the history of the regime from 1921 to 1930, we were prosperous, things were going well, our trade doubled and trebled-it has been cut down by half now owing to many circumstances that I have not time to enumerate-we had money, Canadians were confident of the future, and they wanted men to develop this country. I see the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens): he is one of the prominent sons of British Columbia, one of its most distinguished representatives in this house. How fervently he pleaded the cause of Vancouver and other ports of British Columbia for improvements. He has contributed, and the King government contributed to make Vancouver what it is today, the second port in Canada. Every decent city wanted to have a hotel, a railway hotel, like they have in the mother country. The two outstanding instances that have been given of the construction of hotels have been a success, that is, as far as hotels can be a success managed by railway companies. We had first that unique hotel, the Chateau Frontenac at Quebec, unique in the world by the site it occupies and the enchanting surroundings. The Chateau Frontenac has been a great success, it is today one of the great hotels of the world. Then when Sir Wilfrid Laurier advocated the taking of a small part of Major Hill park here for the construction of the chateau there was a scandalous scene in this house, I remember the Conservative whip our late friend from Leeds, how scandalized he was at the idea of building a hotel here. But in those days the best hotel we had was the old Russell House, forty or fifty years of age. The Chateau Laurier has not been a paying enterprise, but it filled a long-felt want; the Prime Minister himself has been among the first to acknowledge its usefulness, and during the empire conference we were very happy to have such a hotel here. The Royal York in Toronto is another instance, a credit to the country and to the enterprise of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The other railway hotels, in Winnipeg, Vancouver, and throughout the west would all be accepted as quite rational and normal were we living under rational and normal conditions. But we are not, we are facing hard times, the result no doubt primarily of the war, but subsequently of wrong fiscal policies that we have adopted in Canada, policies which have been condemned by the League of Nations, as the curse not only of this country but of every country in the world. We have now economic
warfare displacing the oldtimc warfare of 1914 to 1918.
The Prime Minister in bringing in these proposals is merely trying to get back to the old Liberal doctrine, to freedom of trade, to knock down the barriers, to get back to lower tariffs. No trade can be carried on while you have these obstacles and barriers in the way, either high tariffs or disturbance of exchange or the gold standard or depreciated currency, on which our friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce has given us such enlightening addresses in this house and which I for myself have studied with great interest. These are all factors in bringing about the situation we now occupy. But, Mr. Speaker,
I contend as a result of whatever experience I have had that Canada's situation is different from that of the densely crowded countries of Europe. We have an immense territory, we have only begun to develop the resources of Canada. We have under the plough only ten per cent of the western country known to the farmer. We have in our own province hundreds and thousands of miles that have not yet been touched. We have here a country which is unparalleled on the face of the earth, we must have a policy that suits this country, and the policy that suits this country is a policy of free trade except for the demands of revenue. We must have revenue, and since we do not want to accept direct taxation we must have a revenue from tariffs to meet our requirements. Now the higher our tariffs the lower our revenue. We are resorting now to direct taxation, we have it on postage stamps, we have it on everything. Our revenue is falling off, it is going to fall off more. Where will the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) be when ho presents ids next budget speech? If these agreements are implemented with Great Britain and the other countries our revenue will again fall off. So there is only one policy as far as I have been able to ascertain, that is a policy of tariff for revenue purposes only, a tariff that will develop all our industries, and principally and primarily our agricultural industry. We have four basic industries in which Canada is in the lead, cannot be beaten in the world; they are, agriculture, mining, the forest industries and the fisheries. With these immense expanses of water that we have, with these hundreds of thousands of acres of land, with these forests and the riches that are found in our soil our position should be of the strongest. I remember the day fifteen or twenty years ago when cobalt ore was
The Address-Mr. Marcil

discovered in northern Ontario. See where northern Ontario stands to-day in the mining field. In mineral production, Canada stands, I think, second or third in the world, and we have only just begun. I do not know how we stand at present but we did stand fourth or fifth in world trade, with our small population. There are immense potentialities within our grasp, but we should be moderate and reasonable, we should follow the old policy of give and take and not imagine that we can sell unless we buy. If we close our markets to others, others will close their markets to us; the only way in which we can get trade is to look after trade and buy from others and let others buy from us. There were reasons for raising certain of our tariff items against the United States. The United States has, in my view, raised its tariffs beyond all common sense in many instances, and the result is that their foreign trade has dwindled to almost nothing, about $17 per head. Sixty-seven countries in the world have practically placed an embargo on American products and have practically no dealings with the United States. We do not want to be in that position, and I hope that after the discussion has taken place on these proposals which are now before us, the Canadian people will have begun to realize that something has been done for them at last, because nothing of any practical good has been done so far. It is true that we have given a few days' employment here and there. But, on the other hand, we have in the province of Quebec alone 1,500 municipalities which are unable to meet their obligations. This year for the first time in thirty years the province of Quebec has a deficit. Other provinces have also run into debt; four or five of them are unable to meet their obligations, and we have to vote money here to help them out. What has been done for Canada during the last two and a half years, and what is being done for Canada now? Are we satisfied with our work? There are
700,000	men out of employment in this country to-day. Are those who form the majority in this house satisfied that they have implemented the promises which they made to the people in the good old summer time of 1930?
There are, I admit, conditions that are insurmountable. I want to be fair to the Prime Minister. He has given an example of industry which I have never seen surpassed and rarely equalled in this house, but unfortunately in making his proposals he forgot one important point, and that is that it takes two to make a bargain. Though his intentions

were good, though he intended to do many good things, he found it impossible to carry out his promises. The people in my part of the province come to me day after day and say: "You are an old member of the house; can you not bring on an election and give us a chance to have a change in the fiscal policies of this country? Because we are starving; we have no money, no work, no market, nothing with which to clothe our children. An appeal was made in the Montreal Gazette two or three days ago by an Anglican clergyman on the coast of Gaspe for clothing to be sent by the people of Montreal down to Gaspe to clothe the poor children there. That is the condition in the oldest part of Canada, a part which was discovered four hundred years ago by Jacques Cartier, a section of this country which has known all that is good and bad in Canada. The people in that part of my province are in such dire straits that they are unable to clothe and feed their children. And so it is throughout the land.
I sincerely hope, Mr. Speaker, that some good will come out of these conference agreements, but from the extracts that I have read I have many misgivings as to their results. Anyway it will take time, and time alone is the arbiter in these questions. In the meantime I trust that the government will not rest satisfied with merely giving relief to those of our people who are in want and distress, making paupers of them all, but rather that they will find a way to give them work instead of merely a dole.
Reference is made in the speech from the throne to the St. Lawrence waterway. I listened the other day at Brockville to a number of speeches on this subject, but if there is a Democratic victory in the United States at the next election, we will probably not hear of this waterway for some time. If the American senate rejects the proposal we may never have to deal with it in our day. It is a far-off question in any event; there is not much relief to be expected from that quarter in the immediate future. If the recommendations of the transportation commission are implemented they will result in a few more thousands of men being thrown out of employment. You see what the feeling is in this country. You see what it was in South Huron and in Maisonneuve, with half a dozen candidates in the field, and in Royal, New Brunswick, and what it is in all parts of this country. I am thankful for one thing, and that is that the Liberal party is not in office at the present time with the same results from its policies; for had we had the same

The Address-Miss Macpliail
policy upon which our hon. friends opposite have been proceeding during the last few years, undoubtedly we would have had the same results. It is a mistaken policy, and I hope that the Prime Minister in his arrangements with the other countries of the empire ' is beginning to undo what he has done, beginning to bring down the tariff barriers so as to give Canadians, as he himself put it, a chance. Well, the time has arrived. Half the term of this parliament has expired. Time flies quickly; parliaments pass rapidly. Today the Prime Minister introduces a bill for redistribution, and we may have an election in twelve months or twenty-four months. But what matters it? Will every member of this house be in a position when he goes before his electors to declare that this House of Commons did what it should have done in the circumstances in which we now find ourselves to give to the Canadian people the treatment and the fiscal policy, the government and the public administration to which they are entitled? I am not thinking of party lines at the present moment. I am willing to support these measures if it can be shown that they are for the advantage of our people, because in my constituency I have men of all parties, of all creeds and of all nationalities who are in dire want. It is a question of humanity; it is a question of coming to their relief. It is a question of finding means to give to Canadians, who are entitled after all to fair treatment, that which they have not had in the past and which they do not possess today either in my province or in any other. We shall probably have some long debates on these empire proposals. I think it is only fair to the Canadian people and fair to this house that these agreements should not be voted blindly. There will be disagreements. No doubt certain members of the Conservative party will have independence enough to show where those disagreements are. They may point out that mistakes have been made. Let us not forget that in these agreements we are tying ourselves down for five years. When we come to negotiate treaties with other countries we shall be up against this five year noose that we have put around our necks. Is it fair that we should hem ourselves within the British Empire, immense as it undoubtedly is, and forget the rest of the world? These are considerations which well deserve the attention of this house before we finally come to express an opinion on this question.
There are other questions to which I should like to refer but I do not wish to delay the house at any further length, except in the
five minutes remaining to cover the remainder of the speech from the throne.
How is the Liberal party meeting the present situation? It has met it by the amendment moved by the right hon. leader of the opposition, to which a rider has been added by our friends in the other corner, expressing general dissatisfaction with the present state of affairs. I hope that when that subamendment is voted down, as the main amendment will be later, we shall take up and consider these empire proposals with the sole purpose in view of helping the country. I hope that we shall consider these agreements deliberately and dispassionately, with no bias, because we have reached the point where Canada must either go ahead or go back. I am thankful that we have in our cities, in the great city of Montreal, for instance, with a population of one million, a law-abiding people, because otherwise what might net happen? See what happened in Belfast yesterday, and consider what might happen in this country if our people were not law-abiding. The people need to be helped and they must be helped by broad, conscientious and patriotic measures which will show that we, their representatives in this house, place the public good above all cither considerations, and with that in view have legislated as best we knew how to find a solution for one of the greatest problems, if not the greatest, that this country has ever had to deal with.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had intended to say
a good deal concerning the second to last paragraph of the speech from the throne, but it has been so well dealt with by other hon. members that I feel I need say very little about it. My eleven years experience in the House of Commons led me to believe that the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) who for many years was leader of the government, was the greatest master in Canada of phrasemaking. I thought that at any time he could carry off the palm for the bringing together of beautiful if sometimes meaningless words. However, after reading the second to last paragraph in the speech from the throne, I feel he must give place to the present Prime Minister. We find such expressions as the

The Address-Miss Macphail
following: " retrenchment and constructive development," " enviable financial position of this country," and " the integrity of industry." That, more than any other expression, challenges my admiration; I should never have thought of it. When one thinks of the watered stock of industry and the callousness with which industrial leaders turn out their employees; when one considers the tariff concessions given year after year and time after time, and adds to that excise protection- a new name for tariffs-and then makes the addition of dumping duties, we come to an understanding of what is termed " the integrity of industry."
Then we find the expression " the resourcefulness of agriculture." I understand that very well. The expression really means that the farmer stops taking the daily paper, has his telephone removed from the house, does without a new winter overcoat, and has his children do without a much needed tonsil operation. The farmer's wife does not get her new hat or new shoes; they are not able to take the little trip they had planned- oh, yes, I understand that.
And then the last expression-" enabled us to take quick and profitable advantage of improved conditions." That is good. Then there is one other I should not like to miss, namely his reference to " approaching prosperity." Of course, if it is on the road anywhere, I suppose it is approaching-unless it is running the other way. That, too, might be possible. The paragraph to which I have referred is such a gem that, really, we ought to see that it goes into every home in Canada. It is too bad that the king's representative had to say it, but it is really rich- in fact, it is the best I have heard in eleven years.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, that is saying a
good deal. Now I should like to refer to the Prime Minister's speech in reply to the one he had previously made. He has said that his government stands for sound money. In that connection his words are as follows:
There is only one thing that can be said about this government with respect to its monetary policy, and that is this: We will stand for sound money.
I believe if he had taken the word "sound" out, his statement would have been equally accurate. I think it is apparent that the Prime Minister and the government-if one

must add the qualification-do stand for money., I believe he stands for high interest rates, for deflation, for the payment of debts with dear money-debts which were contracted with money which was worth about half what it is now, and at a time when commodities were worth about twice their present value. The government and the Prime Minister stand for money, because the terrific taxation in this country does not bear very heavily upon the moneyed classes, but bears most heavily upon the backs of the masses.
In contrast to the position taken by the Prime Minister, either that he stands for sound money or for money, I want to say quite frankly that I stand for the people. I stand for those farmers who this year have worked and were not only underpaid, but, as a matter of fact, were not paid at all. I believe it is not inaccurate to say that there is not a farmer in the province of Ontario who this year can earn his taxes from the proceeds of the land he has cultivated. True, he might pay them from accumulated capital, or by selling off some of his young stock which he should not have to sell, and the selling of which impoverishes him for the next year. He might pay his taxes by doing without things that he needs, or by borrowing. I repeat however, it is not inaccurate to say that there is not a farmer in Ontario who this year will pay his taxes from the earnings of his land. I am very proud to stand for that type of person. In the class I include not only the farmers, but also the unemployed. Those people constitute a disinherited class, and it is a very large class in Canada. One does not need to quote figures, but we may have noticed that the leader of the opposition said there were 500,000 unemployed; probably 700,000 would be closer to the number. There is in Canada this great disinherited class which in these fall months must face the winter with fear. Some one must stand for them. I think a great many hon. members in this house are seeking to serve them. I believe we are all sympathetic. I think the Prime Minister is sympathetic-but unfortunately, sympathy is not enough. We must stand for a money policy, and a general national policy which will bring this disinherited class into its inheritance again, a policy which will make of them people like ourselves who are not fearful that they will not get something to eat or have a house to live in, or clothes to wear.

The Address[DOT]-Miss Macphail
So the Prime Minister is exceedingly welcome to his statement that he stands for a sound monetary policy if by that expression he means the monetary policy he has been pursuing. Then later in his address, he stated that there were people going around the country-he referred to them as soap box orators, communists, and socialists-who will endeavour to arcuse the passions and prejudices of the people, and who will carry to them tales of new nostrums and remedies that will cure all the economic evils of the day. I say to the Prime Minister that I suspect I am one of the soap box orators to whom he has referred. I have no apologies to make, but would say, to quiet the fears of the Prime Minister, that I did not stir the prejudices or passions of the people. He has done that already. Does he not know that the kind of speech he made the other day is the very thing that does stir the prejudices and passions of the Canadian people We picture the Prime Minister in his absolute, assured, and complete comfort this winter holding out to the unemployed the one hope that if they emerge from the present crisis, they will be better people, and that they will be strengthened by the fires of adversit}7.
I have some further remarks concerning soap box orators. While visiting Smith College for a period of three days, just before the house met, I met a man named Mr. Muste who was the head of a labour college. This gentleman would compare favourably with our own J. S. Woodsworth-that sort of man. In his remarks he said that people were now ready to listen to anybody, and that is why he was there. He felt that they would not have had him some years ago. Doctor Neil-son, president of Smith College, said that when more and more people had less and less, they were more and more ready to listen to ideas. And so, if the Prime Minister wishes to call us soap box orators, I am quite content. At any rate, the people of Canada have been looking for a lead. They have been looking for ideas which they thought would be of some use to them if put into practice, and primarily they have been looking to the leader of the government. I doubt whether in recent Canadian history the people have turned so unanimously to one man for help as they turned to the Prime Minister just two years ago. They have been listening all these months for something w'hich, to them, might have the ring of reality, but they have been disappointed-just this talk about the fires of adversity. I hope he will not hear what the people are going to think of it. Surely he does not know the
suffering of the Canadian people, the mind of the Canadian people today. And failing to hear from the Prime Minister, the things which the people feel that he ought to have said, things that need to be said, they have turned a listening ear to the leader of the opposition. All summer I myself have been waiting for him to say something that meant something. One thing I have heard in this long summer, however. The other day I noticed that he had imdergone a conversion, a recent conversion to monetary reform, but it wTas so recent that he stumbled over the words. He does not use them glibly yet. That is why, to finish up with the soap box orators, the people are asking those of us who are saying different things to go and say them, not because they think we are necessarily right but because at any rate we are saying something that fits their case, and they are therefore willing to listen. I have no apologies to make; I am rather glad that we have something to say to the people to which they are ready to listen. We do not have to have a band to meet us at the station; we are not expensive people to have. You can go into little halls where there is hardly enough light to see by, but fortunately crowded with people who want to hear something different from what hon. gentlemen have been telling them. You do not have to assure the people that you are one of them, because if you arc one of them the fact is obvious and if you are not no amount of explanation will help you at all.
Personally I was relieved when the Prime Minister hit upon the word nostrum; I was fearful of what might happen if his indignation did not find adequate vent. I want to discuss for a moment sound money, or at any rate money, whether sound or unsound. I should say that you might say almost anything about our money except that it is sound; you might call it elastic money or vanishing money or apparent money, but it does not seem to me that you can describe our money today as sound. The Prime Minister tells us that it is sound because we are going to discharge our contractual obligations. I do not think we are. I think of the people who contracted debts when commodity prices were twice what they are today, and perhaps three times in some instances, and then I think of sound money, in the language of the Prime Minister, which requires these farmers and others as well to pay back the debts which they contracted with money that is worth two or three times as much as the money they got when they borrowed it. There is nothing soimd about that money; it is ab-

The Address-Miss Macphail
solutely unsound. We have a fixed yard measure, a fixed bushel measure, and fixed pound measurement; but the dollar is not fixed; that is what is wrong with it. I think, therefore, that the money we have is unsound money. Most people realize that it is unsound. For instance, the dollar in 1919 would buy less than half a bushel of wheat; in 1929 it could buy a bushel and in 1931 three bushels, and a few weeks ago it could buy almost four bushels. Surely that is not sound money. Wheat is wheat and does not get bigger or smaller; it is just the same kind of wheat, and a bushel is always a bushel. So that the only thing that was unsound in the whole transaction was the dollar, by which unfortunately we have to measure our wheat and potatoes, our eggs and butter, and our beef and pork, to pay our debts. If sound money, so-called, has developed the situation we have today, and is in part the cause of the army of 700,000 unemployed, if it is the cause of the extremely low commodity prices of all basic products, then surely it is not sound and it is quite time we did something about it.
There is one other thing I meant to mention before and that is that great crowds of young people, men and women, are coming into life thinking they are prepared for it and finding no place in it at all. You cannot see freight trains, even if young men are not supposed to ride on them, that do not carry boys going from one place to another. You pick them up on the roads. I have been motoring most of the summer and have talked to a great number of these boys, just lads, most of them, with high school education, and they are really desperate; they are beginning to talk desperately. It will be a great comfort to them, I am sure, to hear that this trial they have gone through will improve their moral fibre. They will not be able to see it, I am afraid. And if this money we have in Canada has anything at all to do with these armies of young people who have not been absorbed into the economic life of the country, then it cannot be called sound but simply unsound money. It does seem to me that all the people with low prices for the commodities they produce, all the young people who are unable to find employment, and the whole army of unemployed, are sacrifices offered on the altar of sound money; and they are being offered up as a sacrifice to the few, the very few, so that those few, sleek fatted favourites of the god of gold may be specially cared for. Personally, I am going to do everything I can to see that this money system is ended, so that those who are suffering from low com-

modify prices, and the young people who cannot find a place in our economic life at the present time, as well as the army of unemployed in Canada, will obtain relief, let it do what it will to the favourites of the present system.
Eight or nine years ago when the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) stood up in this house and said that money should be issued in relation to goods and services, we all thought that he was more or less off the track. We all had the notion that our paper money must be issued in relation to gold. Personally I have come to the conclusion that the money we use internally need not and should not have any relation to gold. As a matter of fact it has not and we should forget all about it and base our paper money on goods and services. Moreover, it should be issued by the federal government and by the federal government alone, and in quantities sufficient to move goods and services and to raise prices to a point more on a level with the point at which our money was when we contracted our debts. If such money is what the Prime Minister would call unsound money, then I proudly and gladly stand for unsound money. Since we are not children, I do not see why our paper money should have any relation to gold. I cannot get it through my head-I may not be an intelligent person -that you should dig gold out of a mine, get it above ground, write paper against it and then bury it in a vault where it is of no use at all. I must say that that is beyond me; I do not understand it. I do not think that paper money has anything at all to do with gold; it should be related only to the goods and services, the natural resources of Canada and character of the Canadian people. That should be the basis for our currency.
I notice a change in the expression on the faces of hon. members these days when we advocate the issuing of new money in such quantities as to raise the price level. They are thinking a little more seriously about this than they did a few years ago. People say: "That may be all very well, but Canada cannot do it alone; we must wait until it is done internationally. There must be international conferences." To my mind the Canadian people are being fooled along from one conference to another; there is a sort of hope deferred-if it does not come out of this conference, possibly it will come out of the next. The Ottawa Citizen of October 13 contained an interesting article on this very point. Ihe article is headed The Age of Plenty, and is

The, Address-Miss Macphail
by the Marquis of Tavistock, which should make it respectable, if not sound. The article reads:
Undoubtedly one of the worst obstacles which are hindering the eleventh-hour rescue of the world from impending financial disaster is the delusion so widely fostered and so firmly implanted in Mr. Chamberlain's mind,-
We could substitute "Mr. Bennett's"-
-that economic problems can only be solved by international conferences and international agreements. It sounds so plausible, and it is in reality such utter and pernicious dope. There is no great issue where international agreement is less necessary as a preliminary and where international harmony is now more dependent on bold and independent leads from individual nations. The internal value of a country's money is purely a domestic affair and depends on the amount of money in the country in relation to the amount of needed goods.
He finishes by saying:
There is absolutely nothing in trade conditions at home or abroad-
Speaking of England-
-that prevents us adopting an enlightened monetary policy ahead of other nations or exposes us to dangers and evils in any degree comparable to those which are at present in being or loom not far ahead.
That reads like sense.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is sense.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, it is. I wonder if the members of the government read things like that? If they do, how can they go on stating that there can be no money unless so much gold is dug out of the ground in order to issue paper against?
I do not think the chartered banks of Canada should have the right to issue money. I am now referring to their right to issue and not to the apparent money which they do issue in such large quantities. This same opinion is held by many people. I think Henry Ford states it in an interesting fashion when he says that money should be for the service and use of all the people and the right of making it should not be farmed out to private interests like sandwich booths at a picnic. I think that would probably prove a little more profitable than running a sandwich booth, but it is really the same idea.
I have been reading the Toronto Saturday Night all through the year because of the very interesting articles on money. One of John Collingwood Reade's articles contains the following:
Now that ninety per cent of our transactions are conducted with credit money, the making and destroying of which must await the convenience of private groups-who do not, for the most part understand the engines they control
-human life and happiness and its right to the fruit of its own toil depend on the blind workings of the credit system. The system holds the loyalty of its victims-
That is a well chosen word-
-mainly because of the mystery surrounding it and enjoys the sanctity derived from nothing but long usage.
That is putting it very clearly. I should like to quote from Sir William Beveridge. At one time I was almost against titles, but since we have got into this monetary reform business I feel that one can mouth with confidence such titles as the Marquis of Tavistock and Sir William Beveridge. Sir William says:
The crisis of today represents a failure to manage credit, to avoid alternate inflation and deflation of purchasing power. There is a flaw in our machinery for making and unmaking purchasing power; it is not under control.
I shall quote further from an article referring to Mr. J. M. Keynes, and I do this for the benefit of the Prime Minister. The article reads:
Mr. J. M. Keynes marvels at the "rubbish a public man has to utter today if he is to keep respectable. Serious and sensible bankers have to go about assuring the world of their conviction that there is no serious risk of deflation, when, what they really mean, is that they cannot see good enough reason for daring to hope for it."
We may be drawing close to the time when one can be both intelligent and responsible in making utterances with reference to money. When that day comes it will be much easier to listen to certain speakers.
The banks not only have the legal right to issue money, but they have the further privilege of issuing ninety-six per cent of all the money used in Canada. We are told that the banker's pen makes it sound money. Is that not interesting? The Dominion government should issue its own money and put it out in relation to goods and services to be used in the day to day expenditures of the government. This could be done in connection with the St. Lawrence waterway. I do not want to see this project carried out with money borrowed against which interest will be charged. Let the federal treasury issue new money and put it in circulation. If it were done in that way, we could advocate the completion of this project, but we cannot do so when it means that further debt will be placed on the people to provide transportation facilities when what we lack is not transportation facilities but something to transport.
The Prime Minister does not need to sneer it the printing presses. I should like to ask



The Address-Miss Macphail
the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) how these nice, new, crisp federal notes are got out if the printing press is not used. I hope the Minister of Finance does not have to sit up and do them all by hand, but I suppose since the bankers can print bills so also can the Minister of Finance. I was going to say that I resented that statement by the Prime Minister, but I realize it is too amusing to be resented. However, I do resent the way in which he stands up in this house and lectures us and tells us everything about everything; it is just too much.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is amusing at any rate.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Though we have "sound money," we are caught between the American gold dollar and the British paper pound. We are neither fish, fowl or good red herring, and yet we are paying the price both ways.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is sound.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The Prime Minister's fury in denouncing unsound money reminds me of Ramsay MacDonald's hysteria during the last British elections when he went around waving German marks. I think those hardheaded Scotch people should have known better than to be carried away by his statements. He told them what a dreadful thing would happen to England if she went off the gold standard, and then he became the Prime Minister of the government which took the country off that standard almost at once. If possible, I should like to help the Prime Minister and save him from apoplexy, and I shall quote Mr. J. Maynard Keynes on England's going off the gold standard. Mr. Keynes, who is considered to be a very able economist, says:
Moreover, there has been a still recent and, in my judgment, most blessed event, of which we have not yet had time to gain the full benefit. I mean Great Britain's abandonment of the gold standard. I believe that this event has been charged with beneficent significance over a wide field. If Great Britain had somehow contrived to maintain her gold parity, the position of the world as a whole today would be considerably more desperate than it is, and default more general.
Somebody ought to tell the Prime Minister that. I wanted to take time, but I will not do so, to quote again from John Collingwood Reade, as he gives several ways in which we could get more money into circulation. One is by lessening the amount of gold behind each dollar, and the other, and the one I like myself, is simply iby the federal government printing the money and putting it out into circulation in quantities that will raise the

price level in Canada to something approaching the 1928-29 price level, and also putting: us on a level with the British paper pound. May I say, since I have not much time to go into the matter, that the array of inviting markets which the Imperial conference has opened up to us but which we cannot enter because of exchange, reminds me of how the unemployed must feel when they walk past a window full of luscious food. They have an empty stomach and the merchant has the food, but as they have not any money they cannot get food into the stomach. The conference says: You can. sell hundreds of thousands of pounds of bacon, so many cattle and so many this and that in England; think of the wonderful things we have done for you! But the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance know

and they must know because they are intelligent men or they would not be where they are-that the farmer cannot enter that market when the British paper pound is worth $3.80 and when we are losing twenty-five cents on every dollar's worth of produce that we send over there. I was sorry about this because it adds to the worries of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) who, heaven knows, had enough before. He brought all the experts together in the Royal York hotel and they had a three days' conference. That they were experts, not dirt farmers, does not need to be enlarged upon, since they were at the Royal York hotel. They went on to tell what we were to do, and one oif the experts, in an interview which he gave to the Toronto Daily Star on August 31, 1932, said: "The future is bright for the Canadian farmer." Then they went on to tell how the farmer was to get into this bright market and about the bright future. He was to do it by using more extensively the scientific information which the expert possesses. You know, after all, the farmers have been a long-suffering people. We have had an immigration policy, which was referred to by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) this afternoon, which brought in, not manufacturers, not merchants, not doctors and not lawyers, but farmers, to put them on the land to produce more stuff. Then the experts show us how to produce not only what we produced before (but more than that. But nobody knows what we are going to do with what we produce. The Imperial conference tells us that we are to sell it on the British market with a 25 per cent exchange against us. I should like someone to try that. Will some Conservative farmer try sending his bacon, his apples, his cattle, at this time to the

The Address-Miss Mncphail
British market? The result will be very interesting. The cooperative live stock shippers made a compact more than a year ago with the Scottish British Cooperative in the old country to send them cattle and they toiled manfully to do this. A couple of months ago Mr. W. A. Amos went over there to pay the loss in exchange which amounted to several thousand dollars.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They did not send cattle.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Let the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) make his own speech. He knows all about cattle. It does not matter whether they are finished or store cattle or live or dead cattle, we are paid in the English paper pound and when we try to convert it into Canadian currency we are losing 25 per cent of the price of the stock in Liverpool. Someone suggests that they lose 318 a head on steers. I know on one shipment of cattle amounting to seven hundred head that went from the stockyards in Toronto last summer just before we did not meet the Prime Minister in Ottawa, they lost $10,008 on that deal in exchange. If the same deal were to go through now with the cattle at S80 a head, they would lose $14,000 in exchange. For any responsible minister of the crown, able and intelligent men as ministers of the crown are-and I say that with all respect and deference-to stand in his place and say: Here is a great market for the Canadian farmer, is sheer nonsense. If they' want us to go on respecting them they had better admit this. There is nothing quite so provoking about a person as to be always right; that is the thing about the Prime Minister that infuriates me.
May I quote from Lord Rothermere-and I hope I may have time to do so, because the Prime Minister holds Lord Rothermere in such high regard that he met him in preference to meeting a delegation of four thousand farmers from two provinces, one-third of whom had been his ardent supporters, a delegation that was supported by the clergy of the province of Quebec and by a very large number of prominent citizens, not farmers, from the province of Ontario. But the Prime Minister was so busy-and one does not wonder at that-that he could not meet them, and his Minister of Agriculture was so overcome with work that afternoon he could not come down for half an hour. However, Lord Rothermere was honoured by an interview which we were not honoured with, although we had tried to make the arrangement on the 24th of May and had made about six contacts with the Prime Minister between that time and the
date of our coming. Lord Rothermere, when speaking of the exchange situation, said:
Canada's being on the gold standard and haying her currency "linked*' with that of the United States rather than Great Britain, was leading to "a slow assassination of the Dominion's trade and industry."
If he really got that through the Prime Minister's head, I do not regret that he had the interview. He ends up by saying:
Regarding Canadian currency, Lord Rothermere said:	"Canada's efforts to keep her
currency linked with that of the United States will mean slow assassination of the Dominion's trade and industry. Canada has a great future within the empire, but she can have none as an appanage of America."
I agree wholly with Lord Rothermere on currency. The odd thing about the Imperial conference which met here was that while they' devoted a great deal of time to trying to work out trade agreements, most excellent trade agreements, if they could be used, they dismissed the whole problem of exchange and money with a pious resolution, a resolution which said that interest rates should be lowered and that price levels should be raised, and they let it go at that.

And they expect
Providence to do that.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, but since we were given intelligence I fancy we shall be left to do it ourselves.
I would say in closing that while there are many other problems and while I do not maintain that an issue of new money based upon the resources of Canada would solve all our problems, I do say that if the federal government with the machinery they have could be induced to put a large issue of new money out into circulation without interest, it would do very much to raise the price of basic commodities in this country and it would lower our money to the level of the value of the British pound sterling, thereby enabling us to enter and make use of the market so aggressively displayed by the Prime Minister yesterday'.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although this session has been called, as the speech from the throne says, for the purpose of approving the agreements that were entered into at the Imperial conference, I feel that there is a duty devolving upon me, not only to give expression to the views that are held by the people in the constituency that I represent, but also to let the government know what in my opinion is the proper thing to do to overcome the adverse

i92
The Address-Mr. McKenzie
conditions which prevail in the country at this time.
In the governor general's speech, delivered on the 6th of October, there are three clauses to which I should like to give some attention, and one in particular that I shall go into in more detail. The first relates to the Imperial conference. That is of considerable importance and will be taken up in the house as a separate subject of debate. We had yesterday the explanations of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) regarding that conference, but I could not help noticing that as he was announcing his views concerning it, when he came to an item where there was an apparent reduction in tariff, he would look around among his supporters as much as to say, "Give me a little applause now." I could not help but think of the expression of Sir Arthur Salter with regard to Mr. Baldwin. Immediately after the conference concluded Sir Arthur Salter was reported to have said he believed that the Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin could be classed as one of the great Liberals of today. I wonder if the Prime Minister would not like to have Sir Arthur Salter, or some other distinguished man, say something like that about himself.
The hon. member who has just spoken (Miss Macphail) said she could not see that very much benefit could possibly accrue to the farming interests from the Imperial conference. We, in the west perhaps place too much emphasis upon wheat, but, Mr. Speaker, the very fact that wheat today is worth 11 cents a bushel less than it was the day the Imperial conference closed does not give us hope that much benefit can come to us from the Imperial conference. So much, then, for the Imperial conference, which we will have an opportunity of discussing a little later.
The next clause in the speech from the throne deals with the royal commission's report on railways and transportation. We are pleased indeed-I am, and the people I represent, I am sure-that this report does not attempt to impose a private monopoly upon us in connection with the railways. We are pleased that public ownership, as far as our railways are concerned, has been confirmed. Indeed, I might go further and say that public opinion in the part of the country from which I come would not permit of a monopoly in our railways, nor would it permit of a sale, or even a lease, of our publicly owned railway to the privately owned institution. In connection with that report I do not know whether this government will have anything to do with the question of buses, but I believe

the time has come when whatever government has the power of dealing with bus services should see to it that our railways, which are such large employers of labour, get a fair deal in connection with the bus service, especially in regard to the long haul.
The next paragraph deals with unemployment. Since two years ago last month, when we were called here for the short session for the purpose of ending unemployment, a great deal has been said on that question. It almost seems like threshing over old straw to speak of it further. But I am going to say one thing, that I want to impress upon this government. I believe I said it a year or two ago, but I want to impress it upon them again. It is this:	that there is as
much labour employed in the production of S100 worth of farm products, grain or whatever it may be, as there is in the production of manufactured products of equal value. For that reason the solution of this problem of unemployment, our economic problem as it exists today, will not be reached I think until there is an improvement not only in agriculture but in the other basic industries of the country. We must begin with the basic industries. Our manufacturing industries apparently are able to look after themselves fairly well for the reason that they are able to close down and discharge their employees. But we cannot have improved conditions unless we improve the condition of the primary producer. One reason why our manufacturing industries are idle today in spite of high tariffs is that the farmers have no buying power. I have here a clipping that I would like to read, taken from the Financial Post early in this year. It is headed:
Business Disappears
After two years of depressed prices for all farm products, and the third failure of crops in southern Saskatchewan, farm implement manufacturers in Canada approach 1932 possibilities in a very chastened spirit. With sales in 1931 of tractors at 873, combines at 178 and threshers at 493 for the prairie provinces, the situation must be almost bewildering to manufacturers. In previous years the sales were as follow's:	tractors, 17,143 in 1928,
14,557 in 1929, and 9,108 in 1930; combines, 3,657 in 1928, 3.295 in 1929, and 1,614 in 1930; threshers, 6,247 in 1928, 2,095 in 1929, and 2,034 in 1930.
In fact this business has for the time being almost entirely disappeared.
That proves, Mr. Speaker, that protection is not a remedy for the economic condition that exists today. Our industries are in a deplorable condition, as well as the farmers.

The Address-Mr. McKenzie
The next item is the one to which I wish to direct a little more attention. It has been dealt with to quite an extent by the hon. member who has just taken her seat. It is the clause which reads thus:
It is a matter of gratification to us all that in those large areas of the west where, during recent successive years, crop failure was followed by widespread distress, this season's bountiful harvest forecasts greatly improved conditions and makes possible a corresponding reduction of relief measures.
Just think, Mr. Speaker, conditions in western Canada as they are today, and the Prime Minister saying that "this season's bountiful harvest forecasts greatly improved conditions." From the point of view of bushels of grain the crop just harvested probably may be considered a bountiful harvest. Estimates have been given as high as
460.000.	000 bushels to 470,000,000 bushels, which in my humble opinion is possibly
100.000.	000 bushels too high. But the important feature is not the amount of grain that is produced. Four hundred million bushels at a proper price would mean a considerable amount, but not with the prices that prevail today. When I left the west at the beginning of this month to come down here, No. 1 northern wheat in the town in which I live was worth 33 cents a bushel at the elevator. That is below the cost of production. Yet they say this bountiful harvest is going to improve conditions, while the farmers are out money on every bushel of wheat they grow. Whoever is responsible for this statement was certainly not conversant with the actual conditions that exist on our farms. I wondered when I read that statement if by any chance the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) was responsible for it. It is very much on a par with the statement that he is reported to have made in the South Huron by-election, and I think possibly that ridiculous statement was partly responsible for the very large majority which the Liberal candidate received in that constituency. A few members of this house know to what I refer. The Minister of Agriculture went into South Huron and, as reported in the press, made the statement that the policies of this government during the past eighteen months had put $36,000,000 into the pockets of the farmers of Canada. Our farmers in Saskatchewan are wondering just where that money is, because they certainly did not get their share of it.
